chunks.text: This is repo-story: the Claude Code skill and the Python scripts that turned each of these repositories into the audiobook you are hearing. This chapter walks the skill itself.

The two after it walk the build scripts that make the audio, and the last walks the tests and the provenance record behind everything. The skill is a pipeline of five phases, and that shape is the one invariant: Survey, Explore, Inventory, Research, Narrate.
Survey reads the repository's README, its manifest files, and its git remote, then presents a short catalog — project name, author, purpose, tech stack, and how much prompt provenance exists.

Explore launches one explorer agent per repository; each catalogs every user-visible feature — exact commands, exact paths, exact defaults — and writes a dossier, one markdown file per repo, into a folder named dossiers.
Inventory reads the dossiers and groups the features into chapters, orientation first, core workflow next, supporting features after, and writes the plan to inventory dot m d.

Research runs per chapter: a code-researcher agent re-verifies current behavior against the source, a prompt-researcher agent traces each feature to the prompts that shaped it, and both write packets into a folder named research.

Narrate writes beats, then sections, then summaries, and finally chapters dot t x t — one section filename per line. That last file sets the order of the audio you are hearing. The skill exists because of one prompt.

In the July twenty-first vendoring session the user re-pasted his own pre-project plan, calling it the kernel of the journey, and the session export preserves it verbatim: "Create a system for turning a github repo into a podcast.
It will explore the content in the repo for: history and core concepts.

The prose generated will generated for a tts engine and will follow a historical arc and also talk about how this repo adds to the historical arc." The same prompt defined the smallest acceptable version: "A process you can hand to an AI with a github url that will produce a reasonably small number of chapters that I can read online." And, answering a separate question in the same plan: "A prompt and an audio output." A repo URL in, chaptered audio out — that is the seed.

Hold on to the phrase historical arc, because the skill as it runs today has deliberately reversed it, and this chapter ends with how. The pipeline splits work across two models by kind: prose runs on Fable, code and research run on Opus.

The main session is pinned to Fable and owns the planning phases: survey, inventory, beats, chapter ordering. Spawned work goes through four named agents in the dot claude agents folder. Three pin Opus for exploration and research: the explorer, the code-researcher, and the prompt-researcher.
The fourth, the narrator, pins Fable, because narration is the one phase judged purely as prose, heard once, with no re-reading. The split is structural, not prose.

The settings file pins the session — model fable, effort level x high, attested by the decision records and recaps, not any surviving prompt — and each agent file pins its model in its frontmatter. Two decision records carry the history.

The first, zero zero zero one, titled Fable plans, Opus executes, drew the line by tier: Fable planned as the strongest synthesizer, and everything spawned ran on Opus because prose volume at Fable prices was not worth it.
It also records rejecting inline use-model-X instructions, because prose drifts.

The live record, zero zero zero two, titled Fable writes, Opus researches, supersedes it: the model generation turned over — Opus became the stronger reasoner and Fable the stronger writer — the assignment moved; the enforcement never changed.

Failure stays loud: if either model is unavailable, sessions fail at the pin rather than silently falling back. Each agent is narrowed to its job in its own file. The explorer is told, verbatim, do not chase lineage or philosophy.

The code-researcher re-reads the source and corrects earlier exploration errors silently. The prompt-researcher is told never to blur its three labels — verbatim, paraphrase, or inference. The narrator gets only reading and writing tools, no shell and no search, because its only job is prose.

These four were not always these four: the July tenth recap names the set as explorer, code-researcher, history-researcher, and narrator, and the history-researcher — which once ran web searches for historical context — was later deleted and replaced by the prompt-researcher.
One artifact carries the handoff from planning to narration: the beats. The project glossary defines them as exactly that.

For each chapter the main session, on Fable, writes a beats file — feature order, must-hit details pointing into the research packets, prompt citations, one-clause transitions — and a narrator agent — today on Fable — expands it into a section.

This replaced an older rule that let Fable narrate small books inline; the first decision record lists that two-to-four-themes, write-inline approach among its rejected options, replaced so planning context reaches the narration through beats rather than inline prose.
The whole pipeline also runs unattended, under a contract in a file named AUTORUN dot m d. In its own words, the plan file is the thinking and AUTORUN is the doing.
It takes a GitHub repository URL, looks for prompt provenance in known locations, and works inside one top-level folder per run, named after the repo.

The build scripts default their outputs relative to the working directory, so changing into that folder makes every default just work, with no override flags. Its constraints are firm. No SSH commands. No publishing without an explicit ask, because publishing is the user's own git push.

Never clobber a prior run. Honor the model split, with the same loud failure. And never pause mid-pipeline for approval — AUTORUN overrides that to present and continue. Now the reversal of the historical arc. It took two attempts.
On July tenth the user tried a sentence-level de-fluff pass, in an understated reportage register, across the finished sections of an earlier run.

The recap records it as reviewed and rejected — it made the content drier without fixing the fluff — and fully rolled back, with the note that future tone work belonged at the beats level, not in word pruning.
The fix that stuck came on July twenty-second, and it changed the methodology rather than the wording. That prompt survives verbatim.

It opens, "the story seems long winded, and a bit too fantastical," says the long form "imposed too much on the readers time, the reader being the reviewer," and lands on the redirect: what the user wanted was "a walkthrough of the features and the prompts that influenced the features as they currently exist." That prompt is the single largest shaper of what you are hearing.
The skill's description became audio walkthroughs of features and the prompts that shaped them. The history-researcher was deleted and the prompt-researcher put in its place.

And the narrate brief gained a paragraph test banning scenic openings, extended analogies, and historical lineage — the rewrite of the prompts folder that produced this very section. Those phases end with text files. Turning text into a voice is the next chapter.

summary_chunks.text: This chapter walks repo-story itself: the Claude Code skill that reads a repository and writes the walkthrough you are hearing. A repo URL goes in and chaptered audio comes out — a shape set by a founding prompt that called it turning a github repo into a podcast.

The skill runs five phases in a fixed order: Survey, Explore, Inventory, Research, Narrate. Survey catalogs the project. Explore writes a dossier of user-visible features per repo. Inventory groups the features into chapters. Research verifies current behavior and traces each feature to its prompts.
Narrate writes beats, sections, and summaries, then a chapters file that sets the audio order.

Underneath sits a model split, governed today by architecture decision record zero zero zero two, Fable writes, Opus researches: the main session and the narrator agent run on Fable, the writing model, while the explorer, code-researcher, and prompt-researcher agents run on Opus for exploration and research.

The pins are structural so the rule cannot drift, and a session fails loudly if either model is unavailable. Beats are the handoff artifact between planning and narration, and a file named AUTORUN dot m d is the contract for unattended runs.

Prompts steered all of it, most visibly a July twenty-second redirect asking for a walkthrough of the features and the prompts that shaped them instead of a historical account — the change that deleted the history-researcher, added the prompt-researcher, and produced the methodology this chapter follows.

chunks.text: The sections are written. Now build_audio.py gives them a voice. You run build_audio.py; it finds every section file, orders them, and turns each into spoken audio.

Voice comes from a single reference recording: name one with the voice flag, or leave it off and the script checks the voices folder — exactly one wav there is used automatically; two or more, and it stops and asks you to pick; zero, and it stops too.

The voice is cloned by Chatterbox, the text-to-speech engine this pipeline runs on. It loads onto a CUDA graphics card, which the script requires, reads the reference recording once to prepare the voice, then reuses that conditioning for every line.
Synthesis runs slower than real time, so a full book is a patient job. The final artifact is book dot m4b, tagged with a title and artist you supply.

Almost all of this machinery predates prompt exporting — it arrives in the earliest commits with no prompt to quote — so its provenance is commit messages and one recap, and I'll say when a claim rests on those. First, chunking.

Text-to-speech does not want a whole chapter at once, so the script breaks each section at sentence boundaries — after a period, question mark, or exclamation point — and greedily packs sentences together up to three hundred characters.
That limit has no recorded prompt; it has simply been there since the beginning. After splitting, the code drops any chunk with no word characters at all.

A chunk that is nothing but a quotation mark, three dots, another quotation mark carries almost no sound, and fed that, Chatterbox can hallucinate — reading back the transcript of the voice sample it was cloned from instead. A voice-sample leak.

The fix, from July third, is recorded in a commit message and an in-code comment, not a verbatim prompt: drop those chunks before synthesis. Dropping a chunk shifts every later chunk's position — a shift that once poisoned the cache. The next feature is why it no longer does.

Synthesis is expensive, so every chunk is saved to disk, and the cache is content-addressed. Each chunk's filename carries its chapter number, its track variant, and twelve characters of a hash over the chunk's exact text, the voice file's name, and the sampling parameters.

Position is deliberately not in the key. Edit one sentence and only the chunks it touches get new names and re-render; every other chunk, though the edit shifted its position, keeps its name and stays a cache hit. Re-run the script and every chunk whose file exists prints cached, skipping.
This replaced a scheme that named chunks by index, where any edit shifted the numbering and silently paired old audio with new positions; the only safe response was re-rendering the whole book.

The script also writes cache params dot j-son, recording the voice and parameters the cache was keyed with, so the transcript builder can recompute the names without loading the model. Each chunk goes to a temporary file, then is renamed into place, so a kill mid-write can't leave a corrupt chunk.

A companion script, chunk_cache.py, maintains that cache. Its migrate command renames a legacy index-named cache into content addressing without re-rendering anything — valid only while the text is unchanged since that render, because the rename asserts the old positions still match.

Its gc command deletes chunk wavs the current text no longer references. This content addressing is the newest work here, from July thirtieth; the decision record that moves narration onto a dedicated writing model leans on it — content addressing makes re-narrating a chapter affordable.

Once a chapter's chunks exist, ffmpeg — the media tool this pipeline shells out to — concatenates them into one chapter wav, and the assembly step stitches the chapter wavs into the single book dot m4b, writing each chapter's start and end time so a player can jump between chapters.

The final encode is A-A-C at one hundred twenty-eight kilobits, plus fast start for playback before the full download. Whatever title you pass, the album tag is always Repo Story, hardcoded. The July second work that set this metadata survives only in the project's done list, not a saved prompt.

Next, build_m4a.py — and here the format changes for a reason. This is the production format: the web player consumes one m4a file per chapter, listed in a manifest, not a single book file; book dot m4b became the standalone, legacy artifact.

The switch traces to the May twenty-second recap, which records the cause as a diagnosis, not a prompt: the deployed player had moved to a per-chapter model, and a restart-chapter bug surfaced because this pipeline still produced one file.

So build_m4a.py re-encodes each chapter wav to its own m4a — sixty-four kilobits, twenty-four thousand hertz, mono — named chapter, four digits, dot m4a, and writes chapters manifest dot j-son, listing each chapter's title, duration, and size.

The manifest's version is a content hash, the first eight characters of a hash over each chapter's filename, size, and duration; change the audio and the version changes, so the player knows to reload. A missing m4a gets a printed warning and is skipped rather than failing the run.

There was no prompt for this switch. It was diagnosed in a browser. Now the one feature here with rich, verbatim provenance: the Full and Summary track split, from the July twenty-first session. It begins with a worry about reviewer time.
The prompt reads: I like how this tells a story, and it is enjoyable to listen to, but I fear the reviewer won't spend the time on it due to the workload they have.

It asks for two buttons beside the transcript label — Full and Summary — so a listener can hear a condensed version and, in the user's words, not have to spend the huge time investment for the arc if they only want the pertinent details. The user gated the work.

A second prompt that same day: don't do anything yet except generate the summary and show it to me. Only after approving a sample did the third prompt land the feature, and its wording set the shape of the pipeline. The summary is good.

Incorporate the UI needed to flip between the summary and full text. Add the summary text as the final step of generating a chapter. The final step of generating a chapter. That phrase is why the summary pass sits right after the full-audio pass in the chapter loop, not off in a separate stage.

In build_audio.py, a summaries folder triggers a second synthesis run per chapter, cached under its own summary variant and concatenated to a wav whose summary name keeps it out of the M4B and out of build_m4a's chapter glob — summaries never enter the book file.

In build_m4a.py those summary wavs become their own summary m4a files, each chapter in the manifest gains a summary block, and the version hash folds the summaries in, so a summary-only change still busts the cache. Audio alone isn't the product.
For the site to play any of this, it needs transcripts and a manifest that ties the words to the sound.

summary_chunks.text: This part is the audio engine: the scripts that turn written sections into spoken chapters. The first, build_audio.py, clones a voice from one reference recording using Chatterbox, the text-to-speech engine, on a graphics card.

It splits each section into chunks of up to three hundred characters on sentence boundaries, then drops any chunk with no word characters, a speakability filter that stops the model reading back its own voice sample's transcript.

Every chunk of audio is cached under a content-addressed name, a hash of the chunk's text, the voice, and the synthesis parameters, so an edited sentence re-renders alone while every unchanged chunk stays a cache hit; the old index-keyed names forced a whole-book re-render after any edit, and chunk_cache.py migrates a legacy cache into content addressing and sweeps orphans.

Chapters assemble into a chaptered book file, and a second script, build_m4a.py, produces the format the player consumes: one smaller file per chapter plus a manifest whose version is a content hash, so any audio change busts the player's cache.
Most of this engine predates the project's prompt exporting, so its provenance is commit messages and one recap — paraphrase and inference, honestly labeled.

The exception is the Full and Summary track split from the July twenty-first session: a verbatim worry that the reviewer won't spend the time, gated on a sample summary, then a verbatim instruction to add the summary as the final step of generating a chapter — exactly where that pass sits in the code.

chunks.text: Last chapter ended with rendered audio on disk. This chapter turns that audio into a site you can open and play. First, build_transcripts.py, the script behind the read-along you may be following right now. Its job is to line the words up with the sound.

It imports the same chunking logic the audio builder uses, so a transcript chunk and its audio are always the same slice of text. For each chapter it re-splits the text into chunks, probes each chunk's WAV file for its duration, and records a start and an end, rounded to three decimals.
Timestamps are chapter-relative: every chapter's first chunk starts at zero. If a chunk's WAV is missing, the script prints a warning and truncates that chapter rather than guessing.

The output is one file, transcripts.json, holding books, chapters, and chunks — and, when a chapter has a summary text file, a second parallel timeline called summary_chunks with its own timestamps. How it finds those WAV files matters, because this is where drift used to be possible.

Chunk WAVs are content-addressed: each is named by a hash of its chunk's text together with the voice and the speech parameters it was rendered with. build_transcripts.py does not rebuild those names from a position number.

It imports chunk_filename and chunk_key from build_audio.py — the same functions that named the files at render time — and reads the voice and parameters back from cache-params.json, a sidecar the render wrote beside the chunks.
Writer and reader derive every filename from the same code and inputs, so they cannot disagree about what a chunk is called.

The base alignment feature has no verbatim prompt; it arrives in an April second commit adding transcript generation, and a May recap records its one shaping bug: transcripts failed to load because the script's default slug, book, did not match the slug the site used — which is why the slug flag must agree between transcripts and site.
The summary_chunks timeline is a July twenty-first addition, implementing the Summary-track request quoted last chapter. One follow-up fix survives verbatim.
From the July twenty-first session, prompt twenty-three: "when summary is selected the time shown in the chapters pane is still the running length of the full length chapter.

this should be updated when summary is selected." Since that fix, the summary track carries its own durations end to end, and the player shows the summary's own, much shorter length when Summary is selected, not the full chapter's. Next, build_site.py, the site assembler.
It takes the per-chapter audio and its manifest, adds the player, and writes a standalone static site.

The current mode is driven by chapters_manifest.json, one entry per chapter; each chapter's id is zero-based, one less than the manifest's chapter number, because it indexes the player's arrays directly.

The script copies chapter audio into the site, skipping files already identical by size, and deletes stale audio that no longer belongs. Two of its details carry sharper provenance. One is the feedback-url flag, which wires in an optional events endpoint and stays off by default.

It has a scar: a scrub of private data once dropped the flag's argument-parsing line, and every site build crashed until a July twenty-first commit restored it — a test now pins the flag, which is next chapter's territory. The other is the favicon, verbatim and in two steps.

From the July twenty-first session, prompt thirty-one reports "one small bug, no favicon," with a 404 on the icon request. The first fix reused an old icon. Prompt thirty-two corrected it: "no use the favicon from their site, not my old wbt icon," pointing at the Next Chapter program's site.

The generator now links the proper icon, and a test pins that too. Next, luinst. The player is not written in this repository; it is fetched. luinst is a short bash script that shallow-clones landry-ui, a separate component repository, and copies one component into place.

Called with a component path and a destination — audiobook slash vanilla into player — it clones into a temporary directory, verifies the component exists, then wipes the destination and copies the component in fresh.

The clone address is overridable through an environment variable; the HTTPS form of that override is a durable consequence of the no-SSH machine constraint recorded in a May recap, not a prompt. The fetched player directory is gitignored.

Next, the one-command builder, build_book.sh, in the scripts directory. It wraps the whole Python pipeline so a folder of chapter text files becomes a standalone, emailable player site. It can scaffold a fresh book skeleton or build an existing folder.
Staging strips leading numeric ordering prefixes from filenames, and if stripping would collide two chapters it falls back to the original names for all of them.
Cache clearing is tiered: a chapter-list change clears the entire chunk cache; one chapter's changed text clears only that chapter's chunks; a changed summary clears only its summary chunks.

Before any expensive work it preflights the text-to-speech dependency and auto-fetches the player through luinst if it is absent. It finishes by printing — never running — the command that would zip the site. The script's purpose is confirmed verbatim.

From the July twenty-first session, prompt five asks whether the build book script can produce something "so i can see this in the player locally for testing." Prompt six insists on its defining property: "no, no server, a local only build. a index file i can point my browser at.

no running server." The build delivers exactly that, inlining the transcripts as a data URI so an index file opened straight from disk works. And prompt eighteen ties the same standalone build to the publishing workflow. Then two small servers for local preview: serve.py and serve_chunks.py.

serve.py is a threaded HTTP server with byte-range support, answering range requests with a 206 and streaming sixty-four-kilobyte reads. It exists because a page opened from a file path cannot seek audio; the browser needs a real HTTP context.

serve_chunks.py publishes a live HLS playlist of chunk WAVs over the local network, marked as an event stream with no end tag so a player keeps re-polling as new chunks appear; it skips files still being written and guards against path traversal.

Both are engineering, from April and July commits; no verbatim prompts survive. Finally, where all of this publishes. There is one target: the parent next-chapter repository's GitHub Pages site. No cloud hosting, no deploy scripts, and the owner does the push.

The retarget is verbatim, from the July twenty-first vendoring session, prompt sixteen: "let's replay the commits excluding all personal info and unnecessary info you found (we're not using aws for instance).

modify scripts and files as necessary to have it custom tailored to our purposes." Publishing became: copy the per-chapter audio, the manifest, and the transcripts into the parent site's docs folder, and hand the push to the owner. Every one of these scripts has a test suite and a paper trail.
That is the last chapter.

summary_chunks.text: This part of the artifact turns generated audio into a playable, publishable site.

build_transcripts.py produces the read-along: it re-runs the same chunking the audio used, recomputes each chunk WAV's content-addressed name through the audio builder's own helpers — reading voice and speech parameters from a cache-params.json sidecar the render wrote — probes each WAV for its duration, and writes transcripts.json with chapter-relative timestamps, plus a summary_chunks timeline for each chapter's short version.

build_site.py assembles the standalone site: it copies per-chapter audio, prunes stale files, carries an optional feedback-url flag, and links a favicon. luinst fetches the player from landry-ui, a separate component repository, into a gitignored player directory.

build_book.sh is the one-command builder: a folder of chapter text in, a standalone emailable site out, transcripts inlined so no server is needed. Two small servers, serve.py and serve_chunks.py, give range-capable local preview and a live network playlist of raw chunks.
Publishing has exactly one target: the parent next-chapter repository's GitHub Pages folder — no cloud hosting, no deploy scripts, the owner pushes. Prompts drove the sharp edges.

The July twenty-first sessions fixed the summary time display, corrected the favicon in two steps, insisted on a no-server local build, and retargeted publishing away from cloud hosting — all verbatim in the record.

chunks.text: After the build and the player, one chapter remains: the proof that the build works, and the paper trail for where this copy of the code came from. Start with a standing rule.

From the July twenty-first session, the prompt is blunt: "you see your directives to test first write code second right?" A later prompt in the same session ties the practice to the written rules: "write it with the prompts and checks we have codified in our rules here." So tests come first, red before green, and every feature in that session's summary-track work shipped with its test in the same commit — one commit grew the bash suite from thirty-three checks to forty-one and added two Python suites.

There is no continuous-integration server and no pytest configuration; the suites are self-contained scripts run by hand. First, test build book — test underscore build underscore book dot s-h — a bash suite covering the staging and preflight logic of build book.
It runs without a GPU or the text-to-speech model, using staging-only mode and a stub Python on the path. Bad input fails up front — no arguments, a missing chapters directory, an empty one.

The happy path asserts real output: chapters sorted, the leading number-dash prefix stripped, markdown extensions rewritten to text, content copied through verbatim. A broken Python environment that cannot import the chatterbook engine must stop the build early, with the remedy printed.
The final checks walk the summary track end to end, down to build transcripts emitting summary chunks with real timestamps. Next, test build m4a, a Python regression that guards one behavior.

Using ffmpeg, the audio toolkit, it generates a silent WAV, runs build m4a in a temporary directory, and asserts that the summary WAV becomes chapter zero zero zero one dot summary dot m4a, with a summary block in the manifest.

Then the part that matters: it changes only the summary track, forces a re-encode, and asserts the manifest's version hash changes. The docstring states the fear plainly: cache-busting must key on all content, not just the full tracks. It is the test-first companion to the summary feature.
Third, test build site, guarding the manifest-mode site build against two real regressions.

With no feedback flag, it asserts the feedback URL is absent from the page, the favicon rel-equals-icon link is present, and the chapter audio is copied; with a feedback URL passed, the exact address must appear in the page.

The docstring names the sharper one: a vendor scrub once dropped the feedback URL's argument definition while the page generator still read it, and every site build crashed. The favicon half is the test-first twin of the favicon fix from chapter three, committed red-green in both suites.

The two newest suites arrived on July thirtieth, alongside the content-addressed chunk cache. Test build audio — test underscore build underscore audio dot p-y — pins the cache-key contract without a GPU.
A chunk WAV is identified by what it says and how it is voiced, never by where it sits in the chapter. Same text, voice, and TTS parameters produce the same key; change any one and the key changes.

The property that makes incremental regeneration work: editing one sentence changes exactly one key while every other chunk keeps its cache hit, and inserting a sentence shifts every later position but invalidates nothing that follows.
Build transcripts must use the same helper, so audio and transcript never disagree about a filename. Its companion, test chunk cache, guards the maintenance commands in chunk cache dot p-y.

It builds a fake book with a legacy index-named cache, runs migrate, and asserts every chunk comes out content-addressed with no index-named file left behind and nothing re-rendered — the file count is unchanged, and a second migrate is idempotent.
Then it edits one sentence and runs the orphan sweep, asserting it removes exactly the one chunk the text no longer references while the survivors and the cache-parameters sidecar stay.

Its fixture WAVs are deliberately thirty-two-bit float — the format torchaudio writes and Python's wave module refuses to open — because a probe trusting the wave module alone would misread a real cache as empty. That vendor scrub the site test remembers is the second half of this chapter.

This copy of repo-story is not the original. It is a scrubbed, commit-by-commit replay of a private repository, produced by the script vendor-repo-story and vendored into the parent project on July twenty-first.

The reason it is a replay, not a squashed import, is in that session's prompt: "I want to keep as much of the history and files as possible to preserve the cross reference integrity." The next instruction set the terms: "let's replay the commits excluding all personal info and unnecessary info you found (we're not using aws for instance).

modify scripts and files as necessary to have it custom tailored to our purposes."

Every replayed commit carries a trailer in a fixed format: Replayed-From, colon, repo-story, at-sign, the original short hash, then in parentheses, "scrubbed vendor replay." The original author date is preserved; the committer date is the vendoring day.
Excluded from the replay: an Amazon Web Services deploy path the project no longer uses, an undeployed infrastructure blueprint, and personal and machine details, left as bracketed placeholders.

The script's verify mode re-scans each replayed commit against a banned-token list, because a scrub that misses one commit is a leak. The prompts drove one more discipline. Midway through the vendoring, the author realizes the prompt exports themselves are a leak vector.
The prompt: "this does expose that we need to scan our prompts also as a source of private data leakage. I suggest removing them." The correction was immediate: "yes, redact, don't delete.

go ahead." That exchange is the origin of the project-wide rule that prompt exports are outward-facing content, redacted inline rather than dropped; the prompts quoted throughout these chapters were cleaned under that policy.
The enumerated leak concerns, f-one through f-eight, were confirmed resolved against the vendored source.

A further prompt called for the README banner declaring this copy the live one and the AWS path retired; another, weighing a reviewer's limited time over convention, pruned the superseded architecture decision records at the flip rather than letting them stack up. The replay is not a claim on paper.

The live git log carries twenty-three Replayed-From trailers, one per vendored commit, each naming the private-repo hash it descends from; commits from the vendoring day forward carry none — they are native to this project. And the chain closes with a person, not a script.
Near the end of the July twenty-first session, the prompt: "do a final check for personal info on all files in the repo that you will push.

if it all checks out, give me the command to flip it public (the gh command), and i'll push it after that." Scrub, replay, inline redaction, final sweep — then a human runs the push. One plain fact ends the book. This vendored, scrubbed, tested copy is the live pipeline.
It is the code that read a repository, wrote these sections, rendered the audio, and built the player for the walkthrough you have just heard.

summary_chunks.text: This last part is the proof and the paper trail: how repo-story tests itself, and how this copy came to live, scrubbed, inside its parent project.
The tests come first by written rule — the July twenty-first prompt reads, test first, write code second — and the suites are self-contained scripts run by hand, no continuous-integration server.

Test build book is the bash suite over staging and preflight: sorted chapter order, the numeric prefix strip, verbatim copy, a broken Python environment stopping the build early. Test build m4a is the summary-track regression: change only the summary and the manifest version hash must change.

Test build site guards the favicon link and the feedback-URL wiring a vendor scrub once dropped. Test build audio pins the content-addressed chunk cache: same text, voice, and parameters give the same key, and editing one sentence changes exactly one.

Test chunk cache proves the migrate and garbage-collect commands: a legacy index-named cache becomes content-addressed without re-rendering, and orphaned chunks are swept. The provenance is the heart of it.

A script replays the private repo's history commit by commit, each commit carrying a Replayed-From trailer and its original author date; an Amazon Web Services deploy path and personal details are excluded, redactions left as bracketed placeholders.

Verbatim prompts drive it all — scrub before public, replay with exclusions, redact prompts rather than delete. Twenty-three trailers verify in the live git log, and this scrubbed, tested copy is the pipeline that produced the audio you are hearing.

chunks.text: Meeting the player. landry-ui is a component library written in plain JavaScript with no build step, and its audiobook player is the component playing this narration right now. This book walks through it in four chapters.

This one covers the player's core: the library screen, the audio model, and the transport. The second covers the reading surface, the third offline listening, the fourth integration and tests. One honesty note, stated once.

Everything in this chapter was built between the second of April and the sixteenth of July, twenty twenty-six, and this project only began exporting its prompts on the twentieth of July. No verbatim prompt survives for any feature here.

The provenance is the commit message, paraphrased, plus a session note from early April that summarizes the work. Where even a commit is silent, the attribution is inference. None of what follows is quoted as the user's words.

The player opens on the library view, drawn by a function named renderLibrary. Each book gets one meta line — its chapter count, a middle dot, its total duration — and a small progress dot: gray for untouched, blue for in progress, green once the book is more than ninety-eight percent complete.
The heading is configurable; the calling page passes a title, and if it passes none, the word audiobook stands in.

That fallback, and a fix so auto-resume stops overriding the library screen, land together in a commit from the second of April, and the commit message is the only record of the instruction. Resume sits underneath the library.
The player writes your position to the browser's local storage every five seconds, again when you leave the page, and again each time a chapter ends.

Two keys carry it: rs-progress, suffixed with the book's index, holds the book time and the fraction complete; rs-last-book points at the book you had open. Load the page with no route and the last book reopens where you left it, paused.

The session note records one rule as a mistake to avoid: returning to the library must delete the last-book pointer and forget the current book, or the five-second save quietly writes the pointer back and pulls you into the book again. Now the audio model, the pivotal decision of the component.
A book is not one file. It is one small M4A per chapter, and a single audio element loads exactly one chapter at a time. The change lands in a commit from the twenty-sixth of April.

The reason survives only downstream: a later repo-story session recap records that the player switched to per-chapter files and that its own build scripts lagged behind the change — a witness describing the consequence, not the instruction, so the why is inference.

Because one chapter is loaded, the audio element's own clock is chapter-local. The player builds a book-wide clock on top of it: the chapter's start offset plus the local time. Finding which chapter contains a given book time is a binary search over the chapter starts.
That model shows up on screen as the chapter panel.

Each chapter is a row with its title, its duration, a progress fill that animates only while that chapter is active, and a scrubber handle; dragging the active chapter's handle seeks live, while dragging any other chapter's handle loads that chapter from its start on release.
The list keeps the active row parked about a third of the way down the pane, and stops steering the moment you scroll it yourself.
The panel also declares itself a CSS container: squeezed below one hundred and fifty pixels wide, the titles and durations disappear and each row collapses to the label Ch plus a number.

That number is the row's position in the list, which matches the chapter's own number whenever the book is sequential. The session note describes this compaction as a built feature — a summary of the work, not a quote.

Next, the transport bar along the bottom: minus thirty seconds, previous chapter, play and pause, next chapter, plus thirty seconds, and a speed button. Skipping preserves whether you were playing or paused.

The speed button cycles a fixed list — zero point seven five, one, one and a quarter, one and a half, one and three quarters, two — starting at normal speed, wrapping around, and deliberately not remembered between sessions. Above those buttons is the track bar.
Grabbing it takes pointer capture, so the drag keeps working after your finger or cursor strays off the thin bar.

While you drag, the fill and the time readout follow you continuously, and if the target sits inside the loaded chapter the audio seeks in real time; only on release into a different chapter does the player load that chapter's file, because loading on every move would thrash the audio.

Small ticks mark where each chapter begins. One verified subtlety: the drag math is still computed against the full book duration, while the ticks and the passive progress fill follow the summary-aware clock that chapter two introduces — in summary mode the drag and the fill disagree.

That is what the shipped code does, and no test narrates it. The two commits behind the bar, both from the sixteenth of July, say drag-to-seek across chapters and hover thumb riding the progress edge — the commit's words, from a push that predates prompt exporting.

Last, the address bar is itself a control. Opening a book pushes a short hash route — a slash and the book's slug, lowercased and hyphenated from its title — so the position is shareable, and an empty hash means the library.

Browser back and forward move the player with them, and on load a matching hash outranks the auto-resume pointer. The routing arrives whole in one commit from the sixth of May, and only its subject line records the intent. Sound is half the player. The words on screen are the other half.

summary_chunks.text: Meeting the player, in brief. landry-ui is a component library in plain JavaScript with no build step, and its audiobook player is the component playing this narration.
This chapter covers the player's core; the book runs four chapters — the core, the reading surface, offline, then integration and tests. The features, by name.

The library view lists each book with a chapter-count and duration line, a progress dot colored by how far along you are, and a configurable heading. The resume system saves your position to the browser's local storage every five seconds and on exit, and auto-reopens your last book.

The per-chapter audio model is the pivotal decision: one small M4A file per chapter, one loaded at a time, a chapter-local clock underneath and a book-wide clock plus a binary search on top. The chapter panel shows per-row progress and collapses to short Ch labels when squeezed narrow.

The transport gives thirty-second skips, chapter steps, play and pause, and a speed button cycling from zero point seven five up to two. The track bar drags with pointer capture, follows live within the loaded chapter, and loads on release into another.

Hash routing makes each book a shareable address. On prompts: everything here predates the project's prompt exports, so provenance is commit-message and session-note paraphrase, and the reason for the per-chapter model is inference from a later recap.

chunks.text: Chapter two. This is the reading surface: the transcript panel and everything that acts on the text while the audio plays. Start with the time-synced transcript. Every chapter renders as a column of chunks, and each chunk carries a start time and an end time.

On every animation frame the player binary-searches those chunks against the current playback position and marks the one whose window contains it, so the highlight moves down the page with the voice. Chunks are also controls.
Click one and the audio seeks to its start and plays; if the chunk belongs to a chapter that is not loaded, the player loads that chapter first and starts there.

The transcript itself arrives as JSON over the network, and it often lands after chapter one has already rendered, so the loader re-renders the current chapter's chunks the moment the data arrives. No verbatim prompt survives for any of this.

The provenance is a commit from June twenty-eighth, "fix transcript not loading on initial page load," plus a lesson recorded in the session notes: a transcript chapter's index must be its sequential position in the audio, not the printed chapter number, or the highlighting drifts from the first missing chapter onward.
Follow mode rides on that highlight. The button reads "follow," and it is on by default. While it is on, the panel auto-scrolls so the active chunk sits about a third of the way down the pane.

What matters is how it gets out of the way: any manual scroll gesture on the transcript — a mouse wheel, a drag along the right edge, a touch move — switches follow off, so a reader skimming ahead is never fought by the auto-scroll.
It comes back only on explicit navigation: clicking a chunk, clicking a chapter, scrubbing the track bar, or stepping between chapters.

The shape of this comes from a July sixteenth commit, "transcript follow — visible toggle, re-arm on navigation, fix scroll math." That subject line names the three decisions, but the session predates the prompt exports, so the user's words are unrecorded — commit paraphrase only.
Next, reading mode. The button reads "read," and it strips the player to the transcript alone.

The back button, the now-playing header, the chapter list, and the bottom control bar all disappear; the transcript goes full-bleed, edge to edge, with a larger base font and a small play-pause button tucked into the panel header.
Again no prompt survives, but the commit trail records the iteration the prompts would have shown.

July sixteenth: "reading mode — transcript-only view." Later the same day: "reading mode drops the control bar." July seventeenth: "reading mode full-bleed — max-width none, one-rem gutter." Transcript only, then lose the controls, then go edge to edge — three commits carrying the steering without the words.
The text-size stepper sits beside it: two buttons, A-minus and A-plus. The scale is geometric.

Each press multiplies the type by one point two five, and the exponent is clamped between minus two and plus three, so the smallest setting is about sixty-four percent of the base and the largest is nearly double.
The buttons disable at the ends of the range, and what persists across reloads is the exponent itself, stored as an integer, not the computed size.

Two commits shaped it: July sixteenth introduced the stepper, and July seventeenth pinned the math with a subject that is nearly the instruction itself — "text size equals one point two five to the n, n in minus two to plus three." No quoted prompt, but no commit in this chapter echoes its instruction more literally.

Then scene-break auto-pause. The source text marks scene changes with asterisk dividers the narration never speaks. When playback crosses one during normal forward play, the audio pauses for two seconds and then resumes on its own — a breath between scenes.
Seeks and chapter changes re-arm the detector without firing it, so jumping around never triggers a false pause.

The hold began at three seconds; a July sixth session shortened it to two, and that change has its own recap note, which records something the commit cannot: changing the constant from three thousand to two thousand milliseconds leaves the file the same size, invisible to a consuming deploy that detected changes by file size, and that had to be fixed downstream by content-hashing the player.

One verified subtlety in the code: the detector always scans the full transcript's chunks, even in summary mode, so in practice this is a full-mode feature. Which brings us to the chapter's centerpiece and the best-documented feature in the book: the Full-Summary toggle.
Two buttons, "Full" and "Summary," sit immediately after the Transcript label, shown only for books that actually carry summary tracks.

Switching to Summary swaps three things at once: the audio source becomes the condensed summary recording, the transcript becomes the summary chunks, and the whole time model moves to a second clock built from summary durations.

This was built on July twenty-first, in a prompt-exported session, so the user's own words survive. The initial request, verbatim: "I like how this tells a story, and it is enjoyable to listen to, but I fear the reviewer won't spend the time on it due to the workload they have.

I propose a new feature." The prompt pointed at a screenshot of the transcript pane — the feature specified against what the user was looking at — and gave the instruction, verbatim: "add two buttons to the right of the Transcript pane label: Full and Summary." The motive is inside the prompt: the reviewer's time budget.

A follow-up added a guardrail, also verbatim: "Don't do anything yet except generate the summary and show it to me."

Then the steering chain. The approval came with an instruction reaching beyond the player, verbatim: "the summary is good.
incorporate the UI needed to flip between the summary and full text.

add the summary text as the final step of generating a chapter." That last sentence pushed summary generation into the pipeline that builds the chapters; the player's job is to consume the summary track and summary chunks the pipeline emits.

Next, a placement correction, verbatim: "move the full/summary buttons to appear after the word Transcript instead of to the left of the text size controls currently." The buttons had first shipped in the control cluster; that prompt moved them to sit right after the Transcript label, and a test now asserts the placement.

Last, the time-model correction, verbatim: "when summary is selected the time shown in the chapters pane is still the running length of the full length chapter. this should be updated when summary is selected." That prompt is the direct cause of the summary clock.

The player now computes cumulative summary-based start times and a summary-based total for the book, with chapters that lack a summary falling back to their full duration; and because the two clocks don't map onto each other, switching modes restarts the current chapter from its beginning, preserving whether it was playing.
Initial ask, guardrail, approval, placement fix, time-model fix — a full correction arc in the user's own words. A player this size earns its keep offline too.

summary_chunks.text: Chapter two covers the player's reading surface — the transcript panel and the features that act on the text while the audio plays. The time-synced transcript highlights the chunk being spoken and lets any chunk be clicked to seek there.
Follow mode, on by default, auto-scrolls to keep the active chunk about a third of the way down the pane; a manual scroll gesture switches it off, and explicit navigation switches it back on.

Reading mode strips the player to the transcript alone, full-bleed edge to edge, with a mini play button in the header. The text-size stepper scales the type geometrically, one point two five per step, from about sixty-four percent of the base to nearly double, persisting the exponent.
Scene-break auto-pause holds two seconds at the silent asterisk dividers, then resumes on its own.

The centerpiece is the Full-Summary toggle: for books carrying condensed summary tracks, switching modes swaps the audio source, the transcript chunks, and the entire time model at once — a second clock built on summary durations. Provenance is split.
Transcript, follow, reading mode, text-size, and scene-break predate the prompt exports and rest on commit and recap paraphrase.

The Full-Summary toggle, from the July twenty-first session, carries verbatim prompts tracing a full correction arc: the initial request, a placement fix, and the time-model fix that created the summary clock.

chunks.text: Chapter three: taking the book offline. One honesty note covers the whole chapter. Everything here was built in a concentrated burst in early April of twenty twenty-six, months before this project began exporting its prompts. No verbatim prompt survives for any feature you are about to hear.
What survives is unusually good for a non-prompt source: a detailed session note dated the third of April that records the lessons, and a commit trail dense enough to narrate itself.

Every attribution in this chapter is a paraphrase of those commits and that note, never a quote of the developer's words. First, what the listener sees: the download button. Each book in the library carries a control that pulls the whole thing down for offline listening.
Press it and the button flips to a preparing state, its text reading "Preparing," its tooltip warning you to keep the page open.

Behind it, a function named downloadForOffline takes a screen wake lock if the browser offers one, so the device cannot sleep mid-transfer, and installs an unload guard, so an accidental refresh asks for confirmation instead of silently killing the download.

Then it fetches the app shell, the page and styles and scripts and manifest and icons, and after that the chapters, one at a time, in order. Each real fetch updates the button with a running count, the current chapter number over the book's total.

For every chapter it stores both the full track and, where one exists, the summary track; the code's own comment gives the reason: offline must work in either listening mode. On success the button settles into a downloaded state with a check mark. On failure it offers a retry.
The structural fact underneath is per-chapter caching. Everything the download fetches lands in a single audio cache, one entry per file, keyed by the file's absolute URL.
Adding a new chapter to a deployed book never invalidates the chapters already saved; the download skips anything already cached, silently, with no flash in the UI, and fetches only what is missing.

A companion check runs when the library renders: it probes the cache for each book's first and last chapters, and if both are present it shows the button as already downloaded. The code's comment calls this a heuristic, a fast approximation rather than proof that every byte is on disk.

Next, the service worker, the file sw dot js, which makes offline work at fetch time. It keeps two caches, and the split is deliberate. One is named audiobook dash shell and holds the application's files; the other is named audiobook dash audio and holds the chapters.
The session note records the reasoning as an architecture decision: separate shell and audio caches, so code updates don't wipe audio.

On install the worker precaches the shell, meaning the page itself, player dot css, player dot js, feedback dot js, transcripts dot json, the manifest, and both icons, and afterward serves it network-first: fresh when online, cached when not.
The audio cache is the opposite, cache-first: once a chapter is stored, it plays from disk and never touches the network again.

One footnote sits outside this repository, and it is current as of the thirtieth of July: the shell handler caches every response it fetches, keyed by URL, with no origin check, so the consuming site's assembler, a build script in the next-chapter repository rather than anything in landry-ui, prepends a cross-origin passthrough to its copy of sw dot js.

Without it, a third-party analytics beacon carrying a per-hit cache-buster would mint a fresh opaque cache entry on every pageview, and browsers pad opaque entries to a fixed multi-megabyte size against the origin's storage quota.

That cache-first audio path holds the chapter's central lesson, and it is about seeking. A cached chapter is stored whole, as one complete two hundred response, keyed by its URL with the Range header stripped.
But audio elements ask for byte ranges, so dragging the scrubber requests a slice, not the file.

A helper called serveRange answers those requests from the whole cached file: it reads the cached response as a Blob, parses the requested start and end bytes, and returns exactly that slice as a two oh six partial response with correct content-range headers.

The lesson is in how it slices, and it is recorded three times over, in the commit, in the session note, and in the repository's own CLAUDE file under performance lessons. It uses Blob dot slice, never arrayBuffer.

Reading the cached file as an array buffer pulls the entire file, seven hundred megabytes and more, into memory on every single seek; Blob dot slice returns a lightweight reference to just the requested bytes.
The documented framing is blunt: the difference between twenty-second seeks and instant seeks. The note preserves a companion lesson from the same days: cache keys must be absolute URLs.
A commit dated the fourth of April fixed the offline cache by storing and looking up every entry by full absolute URL. The download code's shape also records two dead ends.

A commit from the second of April adopted a background-fetch API for downloads, and a later commit the same day removed it entirely; the session note records it as unreliable, with partial downloads, no resume, and stale state, which is why the shipped download is a plain sequential fetch into the cache.

The second dead end was memory. On tablets, early versions accumulated incoming bytes and ran out of memory around four point six gigabytes; cloning the response stream didn't help, because the browser buffers both copies.

The note records the fix as a byte-counting stream wrapper handed straight to the cache, and the button was rewritten several times chasing that crash before it settled. The worker also carries a recall mechanism.
On activate it deletes any cache that isn't one of its two current names, and it evicts two named legacy keys from the audio cache. One is the single-file audiobook from the prior architecture.

The other is a chapter recalled after a bad generation shipped, a leaked voice sample; a commit from the third of July twenty twenty-six evicts it so the fix reaches listeners' already-downloaded caches.

That commit is the one moment in this chapter later than April, and its subject states the reason plainly. Finally, install. The web manifest, manifest dot webmanifest, names the app "Audiobook Player," short name "Audiobook," with standalone display, so it opens without browser chrome.
Background and theme colors are both near-black, and it declares two icons, at one ninety-two and five twelve pixels, both present on disk.

Installability rests on the served page linking that manifest plus the registered worker; player dot js registers sw dot js on load wherever service workers are supported. That's the listener's side. Now the developer's: how this ships into other projects, and how it's tested.

summary_chunks.text: Chapter three covers taking a book offline and installing the player as an app.

One honesty note governs it: the whole subsystem was built in an early-April twenty twenty-six burst, before this project exported prompts, so no verbatim prompt survives; every attribution paraphrases the commit trail and a detailed session note dated the third of April. Four features.

First, the per-book download button, downloadForOffline: one press caches the shell and every chapter sequentially, holding a screen wake lock and a refresh-confirmation guard, counting progress as it goes, and storing both full and summary tracks.
Each chapter is its own cache entry keyed by absolute URL, so adding chapters never invalidates saved ones.

Second, the service worker, sw dot js, with two deliberately separate caches: audiobook dash shell, network-first, for the app's files, and audiobook dash audio, cache-first, for chapters, so a code update never wipes downloaded audio.

Third, offline seeking: a serveRange helper slices a cached whole file into two oh six byte-range responses using Blob dot slice rather than arrayBuffer, documented as the difference between twenty-second and instant seeks; a companion lesson says cache keys must be absolute URLs.

The chapter also records two dead ends, an abandoned background-fetch API and tablet out-of-memory crashes, plus a legacy-cache eviction that recalls a bad chapter from listeners' devices. Fourth, the manifest that installs the player standalone, with its own name and icons.

chunks.text: Chapter four. Adopting the player, and trusting it. Everything so far lives inside one repository. For any of it to matter, a consuming project has to pull a component out. That is the job of luinst, spelled l-u-i-n-s-t, a small shell script.

It takes two arguments: the path of the component inside the repository, and the destination directory in the consuming project. It makes a temporary directory, shallow-clones the repository at a depth of one commit, and checks that the requested component path actually exists in the clone.

Then comes the step consumers depend on: it deletes the destination directory outright, recreates it, and copies the component's contents in. A fetch is a replacement, not a merge. Nothing stale survives, and the destination always matches the repository exactly.

The usual call pulls audiobook slash vanilla into a player directory, and consuming projects gitignore that directory, because the fetch is the source of truth. The clone happens over HTTPS by default, and that default has a date.

It comes from the July twentieth session, the session that flipped this repository from private to public. The prompt that opened that work read: "this repo will serve the site. do an audit on landry-ui to see if it is safe to flip public.

wargame that audit to have as much confidence in the analysis as possible." When the audit passed, the follow-up was short: "run the gh flip command yourself." With the repository public, consumers no longer need SSH keys to clone it, so luinst's default moved to HTTPS the same day.

A later prompt in that session cleaned up the documentation: "use my voice, that is fine. fix luinst https path in docs. then drop them from the todo in the session recap." The SSH form still works, through the LANDRY underscore UI underscore REPO environment variable.

Next, what the host page does with the fetched player. The vanilla embed contract is three tags and one call. A stylesheet link to player dot css. A script tag for feedback dot js, loaded before player dot js.

Then a call to RepoStoryPlayer dot init with an options object: a container element, which is required; a books array; an audioBaseUrl that defaults to "audio slash"; a transcriptUrl; a feedbackUrl; and a title for the library heading. Point those at real data and the player runs.

The repository also ships a React variant, a TypeScript and Tailwind component called AudiobookPlayer, and it is deliberately behind the vanilla player. That is a recorded decision, not a captured prompt.

The session note from early April gives the reasoning as vanilla JavaScript over React for the canonical player, more portable, no build step, and describes the React version as feature-complete but not yet optimized like vanilla.

In practice the React variant still runs the old single-file audio model: one audio element, seeking by chapter start-second offsets, where vanilla loads a separate file per chapter. It has no Full-versus-Summary toggle, no reading mode, no text-size stepper, no offline download.

It does have arrow-key seeking of ten seconds either way, which vanilla lacks. It is the older cousin, kept working and left behind on purpose. One control splits the two variants: the flag button, which a listener taps to report a bad transcription.

The React variant renders it, a warning glyph that turns red when flagged and posts a payload naming the project as repo-story, the type as transcription-error, and carrying the book slug, chapter index, chunk index, chunk text, and timestamp. The vanilla player does not render it at all.
The wiring is fully present: feedback dot js defines flag, unflag, and is-flagged; the init call starts the feedback module; the chunk-flag styling sits in the stylesheet in red.

But player dot js never draws the button and never calls those functions, so in vanilla the feature is wired, styled, and unreachable. That gap is deliberate for now. The April session note keeps it as a to-do: feedback flagging UI removed, re-add when the backend is deployed.
Development tooling sits alongside. Serve dot py is a threaded development server that exists because Python's built-in file server does not honor Range requests, and audio seeking needs them.

It parses a byte range, answers with a 206 partial-content response and the correct Content-Range header, and streams the file in sixty-four-kilobyte chunks. Check-m4b, a Python script with no file extension, is a validator from an older architecture.

It checks that a single-file M4B has its moov atom at the front for fast starting, printing the exact ffmpeg fix command when it does not, then checks for an AAC codec, for chapters, and for a positive duration.
The shipped player consumes per-chapter M4A files now, so check-m4b validates a build path the player no longer takes. It stays in the repository as a legacy tool. Last, the tests.

The suites are Node ES-module scripts driving Playwright, the browser-automation library, resolved from a local pinned copy. Follow dot test dot m-j-s carries contracts covering follow-scroll, reading mode, the text-size stepper, the track bar, and the scrollbars.

It was written across the un-exported July sixteenth and seventeenth push, committed alongside each feature, so its provenance is the commits rather than a captured prompt. Summary dot test dot m-j-s carries the Full-versus-Summary contracts and has a verbatim anchor.

The July twenty-first session that built the Full-versus-Summary toggle opened with the user invoking the house rule. The prompt read: "you see your directives to test first write code second right?" That directive is why the summary contracts exist as a suite rather than an afterthought.

The contracts check concrete behavior: switching to Summary loads the summary M4A and shows chunks that start with the words "Summary one"; the total time reads twelve seconds; clicking the third summary chunk moves the clock to about three seconds; summary mode survives a page reload; and a book with no summaries hides the toggle entirely.

Both suites run against a fixture built by gen dot s-h, which uses ffmpeg to generate silent audio chapters and a synthetic transcript, one book with summaries and one without, precisely to exercise that last branch. That closes the book.
This player, the vanilla one, fetched by luinst into the trilogy site, is the one playing this sentence right now.

summary_chunks.text: Chapter four covers how the player gets adopted by other projects, and the tests that make it trustworthy.

Adoption runs through luinst, a shell script that takes a component path and a destination directory, shallow-clones the repository, then deletes and recreates the destination and copies the component in. A fetch is a replacement, not a merge.

It clones over HTTPS by default, a change with verbatim provenance: the July twentieth session flipped the repository public, opening with a prompt that asked Claude to "do an audit on landry-ui to see if it is safe to flip public," after which consumers no longer needed SSH keys.
An environment variable restores the SSH form. The vanilla embed contract is one RepoStoryPlayer init call taking a container, a books array, an audio base URL, a transcript URL, and a title.
A React variant, AudiobookPlayer, is deliberately behind by recorded decision: still on the single-file audio model, missing the Full-versus-Summary toggle, reading mode, and offline support.
The transcription-error flag button is wired and styled in vanilla but never rendered, pending the feedback backend; only the React variant shows it.
Tooling ships alongside: serve dot py, a Range-capable development server for audio seeking, and check-m4b, a legacy validator for a single-file format the player no longer consumes.

Playwright suites, follow dot test and summary dot test, assert the follow, reading-mode, text-size, and summary behaviors against an ffmpeg-built fixture. The summary suite exists because of a verbatim July twenty-first directive: test first, write code second.

chunks.text: This is next-chapter, the public assembly repository, and the site you are listening on right now is the feature set: a library of three audiobooks about their own making, served as static files with no backend.
This chapter tours the site; later chapters cover its assembly, its prompt trail, and the machinery underneath. Start at the landing page, index dot h-t-m-l.

Its browser title reads "Next Chapter — a trilogy about its own making." The markup is nearly empty; a single inline call hands the player the whole library as data — three books: repo-story, landry-ui, and next-chapter itself. Every book credits the same artist, Brandon Landry.
Every chapter title carries a "Chapter N" prefix. Four chapters per book, each with a matching summary track. That three-book shape is the product of two scoping prompts.

The kernel is verbatim from the July twentieth foundation session, prompt twenty-eight: "the purpose of this project is to create the github page that is the interface to the audio books that talks about the repositories." It named landry-ui and repo-story, and fixed the site as a library of self-narrating books.

The third arrived the next day, prompt twenty-one of the July twenty-first vendored session: "I want to add one more repo, this one: next-chapter... which will complete the journey story of all of it." Two books became three.

The one-sentence description under each book answers a later trilogy-built prompt asking to "add a brief one short sentence that describes each book." The title phrase itself has no dictating prompt; it follows from that trilogy framing — an inference.

Next, the player — one paragraph, because it has its own book. It gives library view, chapter navigation with resume, playback speed, a time-synced transcript with follow and reading modes, and text-size control.
It is vanilla JavaScript, one global named RepoStoryPlayer, no build step: the landry-ui audiobook component, vendored rather than rebuilt.

The foundation session records the hesitation in prompt twenty-eight — "i am still conflicted about creating from scratch a reduced functionality user interface as opposed to reusing the landry ui" — and the resolution in prompt thirty-five: "reuse the landry ui, supersede adr 0002." Prompt forty-three locked the framing: the product is the player and the generator; the demonstration is their composition.

Now the feature built for the reviewer's clock: the Full and Summary toggle. Every chapter ships two tracks — the full narration, around seven minutes, and a summary, under two — with two buttons beside the transcript label to flip between them — the best-documented feature in the repository.
Its origin is verbatim, trilogy-built session, prompt eleven: "I fear the reviewer won't spend the time on it due to the workload they have...

add two buttons to the right of the TRANSCRIPT pane label: Full and Summary." The re-issued prompt added a text-first discipline — "Don't do anything yet except generate the summary and show it to me" — so the summary was reviewed as text before any interface or audio existed.
Prompt fifteen approved it and set the build order: "add the summary text as the final step of generating a chapter." Two corrections followed.

Prompt sixteen moved the buttons "to appear after the word TRANSCRIPT." Prompt twenty-three caught the chapter pane still showing "the running length of the full length chapter" in summary mode; the fix threaded a computed summary clock through the whole time model.

Underneath, one durability detail. The read-along text lives in transcripts dot j-s-o-n, the merged timing data for every chapter. The page requests it with a version key: the first eight characters of the file's own content hash.

If the content changes, the key changes; if not, the browser keeps its copy. No prompt asks for this; it is the repo's standing durable-over-accurate rule — key on content, never on modification time — labeled inference.

One feature is present but inert: feedback dot j-s ships a styled control for flagging a transcription error, with logic to POST flags to a server. The published page never passes it a feedback URL, and there is no backend, so a flagged line is written to local storage and goes no further.

Partial by design: the backend was retired in decision record eight; the feature degrades quietly. Vendored code, no next-chapter prompt behind it. The site also installs and works offline, through a web manifest and a service worker in s-w dot j-s.
The worker precaches the shell files, caches each chapter's audio the first time it plays, and slices cached files into partial byte-range responses so seeking works offline.
Its cleanup list evicts two stale entries: a legacy single-file book, and one recalled bad-generation chapter, chapter one-zero-seven-three, replaced under the same name.

All of it is vendored, no next-chapter prompt behind it — inference — though an earlier war-game of the build plan attacked the worker's same-origin assumption, forcing the in-repo hosting that makes this caching viable at all. The newest feature is the quietest: the page counts its visitors.
The July thirtieth session opens by asking, quote, "is there a way to install google analytics here or something like that so I know who hits this page and when?" The answer was not Google.

The page carries a snippet for GoatCounter, a privacy-preserving hit counter: no cookies, no consent banner needed, recording only path, referrer, and a coarse browser and country — and its dashboard is public, open to anyone.
The assembler emits the snippet from an optional analytics key in trilogy dot j-s-o-n, so the site code has one source of truth and a build without that key ships no third-party script at all.

The same assembler prepends a cross-origin passthrough to the copied service worker, because the worker caches every response keyed by URL with no origin check, and the beacon's per-hit cache-buster would otherwise pile up quota-padded opaque cache entries.

The README discloses all of it, answering the follow-up prompt: "is there a note in the readme that mentions and links to this?"

In the browser tab, the favicon, favicon dot p-n-g, is the Next Chapter program mark.

Prompt thirty-one from the trilogy-built session reported it — "one small bug, no favicon" — and prompt thirty-two corrected the first fix: "use the favicon from their site, not my old wbt icon," pointing at nextchapterproject dot org. A registry key tells the assembler to copy it into place.

Last, the trail a reviewer can audit: provenance dot m-d and sources dot m-d. The first is auto-generated and records where the player was copied from, pinning a commit only when it can stand behind one.

The second is hand-written and pins each book's source — including the rule that this third book is narrated only through a pinned commit, because, per decision record nine, a book cannot contain its own generation.

The exact hash is an artifact of when the build ran; the pinned-range principle is verbatim. The whole layer answers foundation prompt twenty-seven, which asked what mechanism gives the reviewer "an unambiguous breadcrumb trail to follow."

None of the docs folder is written by hand.
A script assembles every file. That script is the next chapter.

summary_chunks.text: This is next-chapter, the public assembly repository, and the static site you are listening on is the artifact this chapter tours.

The landing page, index dot h-t-m-l, inlines the whole library: three books — repo-story, landry-ui, and next-chapter — every one credited to Brandon Landry, four chapters per book, each with a summary track.
That shape came from two prompts: a two-book kernel in the July twentieth foundation session and a trilogy addition the next day, recorded as decision record nine.

The player is the vendored landry-ui vanilla component — chapter navigation, resume, playback speed, time-synced transcripts with follow and reading modes, text sizing — a reuse decided live across three foundation-session prompts.

The Full and Summary toggle is the reviewer's time-budget feature, summaries under two minutes against chapters around seven, driven by the repo's best-documented prompt chain, from origin through two corrections.

Around them: a transcripts file cache-keyed on its own content hash rather than modification time; a feedback flag that is present but inert, saving only to local storage; an installable offline service worker with byte-range slicing and legacy eviction; privacy-preserving hit counting through GoatCounter, emitted from one registry key, disclosed in the README, with a cross-origin passthrough patched into the service worker; a favicon fixed by a two-prompt exchange; and provenance documents recording each book's source, pinning a commit only when they can stand behind one.
The toggle, favicon, and analytics carry verbatim prompts; the service worker, feedback, and cache key are vendored, stated as inference.

chunks.text: Chapter two. The player from chapter one plays whatever a registry hands it; this chapter is how the published site, the docs directory, gets built from three separate pipeline runs. Start with the registry: scripts slash trilogy dot json.

A small configuration file, and the whole plan for the site in data form. It carries a title — "Next Chapter, a trilogy about its own making" — a favicon key, and three books, each naming a slug, manifest path, transcripts path, and one-line description.
Those paths point into per-book run folders under repo-story, where the audio is gitignored but narration text and transcripts stay tracked and diffable.

No prompt dictates this file; it is where decisions made elsewhere — which three books, the site's title, the favicon — get recorded as config for the assembler to read. Next, the assembler: scripts slash build dash trilogy dash site.
It reads the registry and, for each book, converts the chapters manifest into the player's book structure with a function named book from manifest — and here is the design choice worth naming.

It does not reimplement that conversion; it imports the function from build underscore site dot py in the repo-story tree, the same code the pipeline itself uses to build a single book. One source of truth, derived from rather than copied, so the two can never drift.
That is the standing "durable over accurate" rule applied: no prompt says reuse this function, the rule says it.

It then copies each book's audio into docs slash audio slash the slug: every chapter file and any summary file — but only when the destination is missing or a different size on disk, so rebuilds skip unchanged audio.
Then it prunes: any file in the destination the new manifest does not expect gets reported as removing stale, and unlinked.

Only after the copy — which needs the plain names to find its source files — does it prefix every filename with the slug, so a book's first chapter becomes its slug, then slash, then chapter underscore zero zero zero one, keeping three books from colliding in one flat player.

The transcripts from all three books merge into a single transcripts dot json, and its cache-busting URL comes from the content itself: a sha256 hash of the merged bytes, first eight hex characters, as a version query string.
Change the content, the key changes; unchanged content keeps the browser's cache. A content hash, not a timestamp.

Then it copies the player's own files — player dot js, player dot css, the service worker, and the rest — plus the icons folder if present, and generates index dot html with all three books inlined into the player's init call.
This generator writes no feedback URL — which is why, as chapter one noted, the live feedback panel is inert. Two additions from July thirtieth: first, the registry gains an optional analytics key.

When it names a site code for goatcounter, a privacy-preserving hit counter, the assembler derives the endpoint and emits one script tag into the page head; when the key is absent, the page carries no third-party script at all — the site code lives in the registry, nowhere else.
The second addition guards the service worker.
